message:
# Your 24 h LC-MS QC target can't be met with one Waters UPLC-MS

**This can't be done with the one Waters instrument at the cycle time I have on file. It isn't a handling or layout problem: the instrument doesn't have enough hours in a day.** I couldn't get a design to meet the target in two simulations, and I've stopped there. Below are the assumptions, the best design I can give, and what would have to change.

## The basic arithmetic
- 768 products is 8 plates × 96 wells, so 768 separate injections, one after another.
- The only cycle time I have for the Waters ACQUITY I-Class PLUS + QDa is a catalog estimate. It is not your method time and not a datasheet value. It works out to about 3.5 min per injection, or 20,160 s per plate (range 11,520–34,560 s).
- One instrument therefore needs about 161,280 s (**44.8 h**) for all 8 plates. Even at the fast end of the range it needs about 25.6 h with no downtime.
- To fit 24 h, each injection cycle would have to average **112.5 s (about 1.9 min) or less**, including blanks, standards and re-equilibration.

## My assumptions (nobody was available to confirm them)
- **Timing:** all 8 reaction plates finish at the same moment. This is the worst case for your 24 h window.
- **Budget:** unknown, so this is a provisional design. The Waters is already owned, so its line in the cost table isn't new spend.
- **Room:** 6 × 5 m with one door.
- **Hours and staff:** 24 h instrument operation, one technician on one 8 h shift.
- **Hazards:** flammable LC-MS solvents. That needs a ventilated zone and separate solvent storage.
- **Screening assay:** a placeholder of a 96-well fluorescence read after 1 h incubation (allowed range 0.5–4 h).
- **Sample prep:** each product plate is reformatted into an LC-MS plate and an assay plate on a Hamilton STAR, estimated at 300 s per plate (120–900 s).

## Simulation results (model predictions, not measurements)

| Version | Equipment | Compounds/day, typical (P50) | Pessimistic (P10) | Chance of hitting 768 | Layout violations |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| v1 | 1 Waters LC-MS, UR5e arm | 192 | 103 | 0 | 1 (safety: UR5e isn't rated to work beside people) |
| v2 | 2 Waters LC-MS, two PF400 arms (rated to work beside people) | **384** | 206 | 0 | **0** |

- I checked the v2 figures against the simulation: 384/day typical and no layout violations both held up. My claim that v2 meets 768 was refuted, so I've withdrawn it.
- The v1 figures weren't checked that way.

**Bottleneck:** the LC-MS step. The model shows it is the only step that changes throughput. In both versions each LC-MS was only about 46–47% busy. That's because the room layout left the arms unable to reach the LC-MS, so the one 8 h-shift technician made every plate move. Overnight, finished QC plates waited to be loaded.

Fixing that only gets you to the ceiling set by injection time:
- **One instrument:** about 4.3 plates/day, roughly 411 compounds.
- **Two instruments:** about 8.6 plates/day, roughly 823 compounds. That's barely above 768 even at 100% use with no blanks, so it's fragile.

## Recommended cell (v2, provisional)
- Input and output plate hotels
- Hamilton Microlab STAR for reformatting
- Your existing Waters LC-MS, plus a second identical unit **only if you accept a second instrument**
- LiCONiC STX44 incubator
- BMG CLARIOstar Plus reader
- Two PreciseFlex PF400 arms

The catalog-estimate total for everything is about $708k. Subtracting the Waters you own, new spend is about **$551k**, or about **$395k** without the second LC-MS. These exclude installation, service and consumables.

## What would actually make 24 h work, best first
1. **Shorter LC-MS method.** Get the full injection cycle to about 1.9 min or less, measured on your system. This is the only way to keep a single instrument.
2. **Start QC before the last reaction ends.** If plates finish one after another, QC can run as each finishes, and only the work left at the end counts against the 24 h.
3. **Run the LC-MS unattended overnight.** Either use a deep autosampler queue loaded before the shift ends, or place the arms so they can reach the LC-MS. Without this, even two instruments reach only about 384/day.
4. **Second LC-MS (Waters or Agilent 1290/LC/MSD iQ).** This would still need items 2–3 and the overnight loading fix before it plausibly meets the target, and that combination hasn't been simulated.

## Caveats
- No literature or measured cycle times were found or used. All durations are catalog or my own estimates with assumed ranges.
- The screening assay is a placeholder.
- No safety claim here means safety certification.
- If you can give your real method cycle time and when each reaction plate finishes, I can rerun the single-instrument case, and it may come out very differently.

first_reply:
I can't design this cell yet. The deadline you set probably can't be met on one instrument at the run time I currently have on file, so I need your actual LC-MS method time and a few other details first. Nothing has been simulated.

**Why the deadline is tight**
- 768 products is 8 plates of 96 wells, which means 768 separate LC-MS injections.
- My catalog has the ACQUITY UPLC I-Class PLUS with QDa (`waters_acquity_uplc_qda`) at about 20,160 s (5.6 h) per 96-well plate. That figure is a vendor-catalog estimate based on about 3.5 min per injection, not a measured or datasheet value. Its estimated range is 11,520–34,560 s per plate.
- At that estimate, 8 plates take 8 × 20,160 s = 161,280 s, about **44.8 h**.
- Even at the fast end of the range (11,520 s per plate), 8 plates take 92,160 s, about **25.6 h**. That is still over 24 h, and it assumes the instrument never stops.
- To fit all 768 injections into 86,400 s (24 h), each full cycle (injection, gradient and re-equilibration) has to average **112.5 s (about 1.9 min) or less**, with no breaks for blanks, standards, solvent refills or failed injections.

So whether one instrument can do this depends almost entirely on your method's real cycle time. Because the 3.5 min figure is only an estimate, I'll only use a different time if you can give one for your method and say where it comes from.

**What I need from you**
1. **LC-MS method:** your real cycle time per injection, including equilibration, and how many blanks, standards or system-suitability runs go in each plate. Is your instrument the I-Class PLUS with QDa, or another Waters model?
2. **When the 24 h starts:** do all 8 reaction plates finish together, or one after another? If they finish one after another, QC can start before the last reaction ends, and only the work left after that point counts against the 24 h.
3. **Steps before QC:** is there workup, evaporation, dilution or reformatting before LC-MS? If so, which equipment and roughly how long per plate?
4. **Screening part:** what's the assay readout (fluorescence, absorbance or luminescence), the plate format (96, 384 or 1536 wells), any incubation time, and is there a throughput target?
5. **Room:** width × depth in metres, door positions and any areas to keep clear.
6. **Budget** in USD for new equipment. Or, if you're happy for me to go ahead without one, I'll mark the design as provisional.
7. **Operating hours and staff:** can the LC-MS run unattended overnight? How many operators work which shifts, and how many manual interventions per day are acceptable?
8. **Hazards:** flammable solvents (I'll assume so for LC-MS), toxic reagents, and anything that needs fume extraction or separate solvent storage.
9. **Fallbacks:** if one instrument can't meet 24 h, could we add a second LC-MS? The catalog also lists an Agilent 1290 with LC/MSD iQ, estimated at about $214k. Or would you rather relax the deadline?

Once I have these, I'll search the catalog for the remaining equipment and lay out the room. Then I'll run the throughput simulation and check whether the 768 products fit in 24 h, with uncertainty ranges and layout checks.
